title: Akosua’s Prayer and the Unfinished Homework

pages.text: Every evening in their warm compound house in Sunyani, ten-year-old Akosua gathered with her parents and her grandmother, Nana Esi, for family devotion. They sang hymns of gratitude and thanked God, the Supreme Creator of heaven and earth, for life, health and the gift of learning.
sentences: Every evening in their warm compound house in Sunyani, ten-year-old Akosua gathered with her parents and her grandmother, Nana Esi, for family devotion.
They sang hymns of gratitude and thanked God, the Supreme Creator of heaven and earth, for life, health and the gift of learning.
pages.alt: Akosua sits warmly with her grandmother Nana Esi and her parents in their living room during evening family prayer and gratitude.

pages.text: After prayers on Tuesday night, Nana Esi reminded her, ‘Akosua, your mid-term mathematics and science test is on Thursday. Have you finished your fraction problems and your science revision?’ ‘Not yet, Grandma,’ said Akosua, watching cartoons on television and playing with her skipping rope. ‘Do not worry! I will pray very hard tonight, and God will help me get every question right.’

Have you finished your fraction problems and your science revision?’ ‘Not yet, Grandma,’ said Akosua, watching cartoons on television and playing with her skipping rope.
‘Do not worry!
I will pray very hard tonight, and God will help me get every question right.’
pages.alt: Akosua holds a skipping rope in the living room while her closed mathematics workbook sits untouched on the table.

pages.text: Before bed, Akosua knelt beside her mattress and prayed with all her heart: ‘Dear God, You know everything in the universe. Please help me pass my practice quiz tomorrow with top marks. Amen.’ She went to sleep without opening her mathematics exercise book or reviewing her science notes.

Amen.’ She went to sleep without opening her mathematics exercise book or reviewing her science notes.
pages.alt: Akosua kneels peacefully beside her bed in prayer while her schoolbag and unopened books rest on the desk behind her.

pages.text: On Wednesday morning, the teacher gave a short practice quiz to check who was ready for Thursday’s examination. Akosua stared at the first question: Add one-half and one-quarter. She had skipped the lesson exercises on common denominators! Her pencil stayed still, and her eyes filled with tears when she got only four out of ten.

pages.text: That afternoon on the veranda, Akosua showed her practice paper to Nana Esi with trembling lips. ‘Grandma, I prayed so hard last night, and I truly believe in God! Why didn’t I know the answers today? Did God not hear my prayer?’

‘Grandma, I prayed so hard last night, and I truly believe in God!
Why didn’t I know the answers today?
Did God not hear my prayer?’
pages.alt: On the shady veranda, Akosua holds out her quiz paper to Nana Esi, who puts a comforting arm around her shoulders.

pages.text: Nana Esi hugged her warmly and pointed to the small maize and garden-egg patch in their backyard. ‘God heard every word of your prayer, Akosua, and God loves you deeply. Look at our garden. God created the sun, the rain and the rich soil, which no human being could ever make. But what would happen if I prayed for a harvest and left the seeds locked inside the cupboard without planting, watering or weeding?’

But what would happen if I prayed for a harvest and left the seeds locked inside the cupboard without planting, watering or weeding?’
pages.alt: Nana Esi points toward the green backyard garden of maize and garden eggs while speaking gently to Akosua.

pages.text: ‘Nothing would grow!’ said Akosua softly. ‘Exactly,’ smiled Nana Esi. ‘Faith in God is never an excuse to leave our work undone. God gave you a bright mind, caring teachers, books and time. When we pray for wisdom, we honour God by opening our books, practising diligently, asking for help when we do not understand, and taking proper medicine and rest when we are unwell.’

When we pray for wisdom, we honour God by opening our books, practising diligently, asking for help when we do not understand, and taking proper medicine and rest when we are unwell.’
pages.alt: Akosua listens attentively to Nana Esi as they open her mathematics workbook together on the veranda table.

pages.text: ‘And remember something very important, Akosua,’ Nana Esi added gently. ‘In life, even when people have deep faith and work very hard, they can still face illness, money struggles or hard days. We must never judge anyone or think that poverty or trouble means a person lacks faith. Instead, true faith moves us to be humble, honest, hardworking and kind to everyone who needs help.’

pages.alt: Nana Esi holds Akosua’s hands warmly as they talk on the veranda.

pages.text: With fresh determination, Akosua invited her classmates Amina and Tetteh to study together under the mango tree. Amina, who was Muslim, and Akosua, who was Christian, respected each other’s faith and loved learning side by side. Together they converted one-half into two-quarters, added one-quarter to get three-quarters, and quizzed each other on science until every step made sense!

pages.alt: Under a mango tree, Akosua, Amina in her neat white hijab, and Tetteh study fractions and science together.

pages.text: That night, after finishing every practice problem and packing her ruler and pencils, Akosua knelt to pray again: ‘Thank You, Lord, for the mind You gave me, for Grandma’s wisdom, and for my friends. Help me remember what I have studied and use what I learn to serve others.’ On Thursday, she wrote her examination with a calm, honest heart and a bright smile. The end.

pages.alt: In the classroom on Thursday morning, a calm and prepared Akosua writes her examination with a confident smile.

activities.question: Why did Akosua struggle on Wednesday’s practice quiz even though she had prayed the night before?
options: She left her workbook closed instead of studying and practising
The teacher wrote the questions in a secret language
Her pencil broke before the quiz started
Prayer is not allowed on school days
activities.explanation: Akosua prayed sincerely, but she had skipped her fraction and science practice instead of preparing diligently.

activities.question: What did Nana Esi’s garden comparison teach Akosua about faith and responsibility?
options: God gives us minds and abilities, and we honour God by studying hard
Farmers only need to pray and never need to plant seeds or weed the soil
Studying hard means we no longer need to be thankful or humble
Only adults need to prepare for their work
activities.explanation: Just as a farmer trusts God while planting and tending seeds, a student honours God by combining prayer with diligent study.

activities.question: What important truth did Nana Esi share about people who face poverty, illness or hard times?
options: Hardships happen to faithful people too; never blame trouble on weak faith
Good people never experience any difficult days or sickness
Anyone who struggles with money must have forgotten to pray
We should ignore classmates who need help with their lessons
activities.explanation: Nana Esi explained that difficulties do not mean a person lacks faith; true faith inspires humility, compassion, and service.

activities.definition: With steady, careful effort and attention to one’s work.
distractors: Carelessly and in a big hurry
Only when someone is offering a prize

activities.prompt: How did studying together with Amina and Tetteh help all three classmates prepare better than studying alone?
Put Akosua’s journey of growth in order.
items: Akosua prays for top marks but leaves her homework unfinished.
She struggles on the practice quiz and asks Nana Esi why.
Nana Esi explains how faith and diligent preparation work together.
Akosua studies with Amina and Tetteh, then prays with gratitude.
